title: Shoulder to the wheel
told: a fable told under Aesop’s name

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something you really want this year, that you mostly just picture?
options: me too, sometimes. this fable is very old and very kind about it.
then you’ll like what the fable says.
keep this one for when a wish shows up.

steps.line: An old Greek fable, told under the name of Aesop: a farmer was driving his ox cart home along a country road after the rain.
The wheel sank deep into a muddy ditch. The oxen strained. The cart would not move.

steps.q: The cart is stuck. What do you think the farmer does?
o: Begs Hercules to lift it out
Leaves the cart and walks home
steps.why: He stands with idle hands and calls for help from above.

steps.line: He stood by the road, hands idle, and begged Hercules, the mighty hero-god he honored most, to come and lift the cart for him.
Hercules came, and said: take hold of the wheel, and drive your oxen. Call on the gods when you are working, or you call in vain.

steps.q: Why doesn’t Hercules just lift the cart?
o: He’s too busy to answer every call
He wants to punish the farmer
Help works with your effort, not instead
steps.why: The fable doesn’t mock the wish. It says the wish works with your effort, not instead of it.

steps.q: This fable’s moral became a famous saying many people think is in the Bible. Which?
steps.why: It isn’t in the Bible (the other two are, near enough). Benjamin Franklin made it famous in 1736; old collections of Aesop give it as this fable’s moral.

steps.line: So he put his shoulder to the wheel, the oxen pulled, and the cart rolled free.
steps.label: one popular telling

steps.line: Today, the vision board. “Manifesting” grew from an American movement of the 1800s. Research finds the dream works better with a look at the mud.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Psychologist Gabriele Oettingen studied people who only daydream about success. What did she find?
o: They often try less, and get less
It makes no difference either way
steps.why: Pure positive fantasy can drain the energy to act. Her fix, WOOP: wish, outcome, obstacle, plan. The mud gets named on purpose.

say: here’s what i love. the fable never says wishing is silly. the farmer is allowed to call for help. he just has to push while he calls.
that’s the honest part of manifesting. a thought alone doesn’t pull a cart out of the mud. naming the wish, and the mud, and then pushing, does.

steps.q: Which of these is closest to what the fable would tell someone manifesting a new job?
o: Picture the job every morning until it comes
Picture it, name the fear, send one application
Skip the picturing and send a hundred today
steps.why: That’s the wish, the mud and the shoulder to the wheel, all in one plan.

today.say: pick one wish for this year. say what’s in the way, honestly. then make one small plan: when that happens, i’ll…
options: lovely. that’s your shoulder on the wheel.
that counts. naming the mud is a real step.

card.from: a fable told under Aesop’s name
sources: “Hercules and the Wagoner”, Perry Index 291; Babrius, Fables 20: the oxdriver’s wagon falls into a ravine; he stands idle and prays to Heracles; Heracles tells him to take hold of the wheels and goad the oxen, and to pray when he is doing something himself, or pray in vain.
Later English tellings (e.g. George Fyler Townsend, 1867) add the phrase “put your shoulder to the wheel.”
New Thought movement, 19th-century America; Rhonda Byrne, The Secret (2006).
Gabriele Oettingen, Rethinking Positive Thinking (2014) and studies on mental contrasting and implementation intentions (WOOP).
